title: The role of human-cat interactions in shaping domestic cat (Felis catus) hunting behavior (2026)
text: The role of human-cat interactions in shaping domestic cat (Felis catus) hunting behavior. Published 2026. Abstract: Domestic cats, Felis catus, play an interesting role in human society, both as companion animals and as predators of local wildlife. Cats are one of the most commonly kept companion animals, surpassing dogs in many areas around the world, and are frequently directly managed by caretakers. However, cats are also one of the most widespread mesopredators with the ability to impact vulnerable prey species, and when outdoors (both owned and unowned) can cause prey population decline or even extinction. This has led to much discussion among scientists and the public on the proper management of owned cats, and whether possible benefits for their welfare warrant the provisioning of free-roaming outdoor access. The objective of this dissertation was to assess the role of management decisions and human-cat interactions on cats’ hunting behavior, bringing together the perspectives of behavioral ecology, conservation ecology, animal welfare, and anthrozoology.Many efforts have been made to reduce cats’ hunting of wildlife, spanning from population control measures such as lethal population control and Trap-Neuter-Release, to targeting caretaker-led interventions such as reduced outdoor access and increased interactive play in the home. Some methods designed to reduce cat impact on wildlife can raise concern among caretakers, particularly if they are perceived to negatively impact their cat’s welfare. This research focused on understanding the role of caretakers, not only as a mediator of cat-wildlife interactions, but also as partners of data collection on their cats’ hunting and hunting-related behaviors. We relied on citizen science to better understand the perspectives and motivations of cat caretakers regarding outdoor access and hunting (Chapter 1), quantify individual variation in cats’ hunting-related behaviors (Chapter 2), and test molecular methods of scat analysis for detection of prey consumption (Chapter 3).In Chapter 1, we aimed to explore attitudes towards providing or reducing outdoor access, identify specific predictors of free-roaming outdoor access, and identify predictors of hunting behavior among cats that are allowed to freely roam. Using a quantitative questionnaire (N=361), we found that more than half of outdoor cat caretakers were likely or somewhat likely to reduce outdoor access if they lived near busier streets (59%), if more dangerous animals were around (59%), if their cat stopped coming home consistently (56%), or if they knew their cat was negatively impacting wildlife (53%). We found that cats had higher odds of freely roaming if they were older, obtained from the street, living close to traffic, or if they showed aggressive behaviors in the home. Among those allowed outside, cats were more likely to have hunted prey in the last year if they were allowed to freely roam instead of being supervised, or were allowed outdoors between in the morning hours.In Chapter 2, we recruited participants in the United States (N=87) to expose their cat to standardised behavioral assay trials using a wand toy, to measure individual variation in response to the toy and the consistency of their responses over time. We found high repeatability of all behaviors indicative of cat interest measured across trials (mean R = 0.467). We then calculated a composite interest score consisting of all behavior variables, and found significant consistent individual variation in the cats' interest in the toy (ICC = 0.717). Interestingly, we did not find any significant connections between the cats' interest score and other factors of interest relating to their management in the home. This study was the first recorded use of citizen science to quantify consistent individual differences in play behavior of cats, and highlights the importance of assessing individual variation.In Chapter 3, we relied on owner-collected scats (n = 32) from litterboxes and backyards to test whether DNA metabarcoding could be used to detect consumption of wild prey by owned, indoor-outdoor domestic cats. We found only one instance of wild prey consumption, a California vole (Microtus californicus), despite the caretaker not witnessing any prey returns during the 24-hour period prior to scat sampling. Conversely, in the instances where the caretaker reported returns of intact prey by their cats, prey DNA was not detected in their scat. This study presents the first recorded use of DNA metabarcoding to detect consumption of wild prey by owned domestic cats, and suggests that caretaker reports and scat analysis should be used in combination to obtain a more thorough understanding of their hunting of wild prey. Together, this dissertation research provides much needed insight into the role of cat caretakers in mediating cat-wildlife dynamics, such as through their influence on their cats’ outdoor access and behavior, and highlights their potential and importance as partners of data collection when studying companion animal behavior.
